lesson.title: The French Mind
lesson.subtitle: avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir raison, avoir besoin de — feelings as possessions and idioms as thought

hook.title: Why You 'Have Hunger' and 'Have Reason' in French
hook.content: In Topic 15 you saw that French doesn't 'be' thirty years old — it 'has' thirty years (J'ai trente ans). That same mental theatre runs across physical sensations and states of mind! You are not 'hungry' — hunger is a visitor you temporarily hold with avoir: J'ai faim ('I have hunger', cousin of famine). You are not 'thirsty' — J'ai soif ('I have thirst'). You are not 'afraid' — J'ai peur ('I have fear'). You are not 'right' — Tu as raison ('You have reason')! And 'I need' is J'ai besoin de ('I have need of').

footnotes.title: Why 'very hungry' is J'ai très faim
footnotes.content: Even though faim, soif, and peur are nouns, avoir faim acts so much like a single feeling-unit that spoken and written French puts très ('very') right before the noun: J'ai très faim, j'ai très soif!

pattern.title: avoir + Bare State Noun (No Article!)
pattern.content: Notice that in j'ai faim, tu as soif, il a peur, tu as raison, and j'ai besoin de, there is NO article (un/une/le/la) between avoir and the noun! The verb and noun fuse into a single idiom. If you say *Je suis faim, a French ear hears 'I am starvation itself'! Always possess your temporary bodily states with avoir.
pattern.linguist_note: Having a sensation (habēre famem / sitim) vs. being an identity reflects the Indo-European split between alienable temporary states and permanent attributes.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: translating 'I am hungry / You are right' with être (*Je suis faim / *Tu es raison). Temporary states of hunger, thirst, fear, and rightness ALWAYS use avoir!

exercises.prompt: Match each avoir expression with its natural English meaning and literal gloss:
exercises.target_answer: to be hungry (lit. have hunger), to be thirsty (lit. have thirst), to be afraid (lit. have fear), to be right (lit. have reason), to need (lit. have need of)
exercises.meaning: avoir faim (famine), avoir soif, avoir peur, avoir raison (reason), avoir besoin de
exercises.explanation: All five use avoir with a bare noun — never être!

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Tu as raison'?
exercises.explanation: In French, being right is literally 'having reason': Tu as raison.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences accurately translate 'J'ai besoin d'un café'?
renderings: I am in need of a coffee
traps: I want to make a coffee
exercises.explanation: avoir besoin de + noun/infinitive is the standard French way to say 'to need'.

exercises.idea: I am very hungry and you are right
cues: I have very hunger → J'ai très faim + and you have reason → et tu as raison
idea_parts: second clause → et tu as raison
exercises.target_answer: J'ai très faim et tu as raison
exercises.meaning: I am very hungry and you are right
exercises.explanation: Both 'hungry' and 'right' are possessed with avoir in French.

diagnosis.slip: used suis or es instead of ai and as
diagnosis.cue: Use J'ai très faim and tu as raison.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Est-ce que tu as soif maintenant
exercises.target_answer: Est-ce que tu as soif maintenant
cues: you have thirst: tu as soif
exercises.affirmation: You used tu as soif with Est-ce que cleanly.

summary.outcome: Express hunger, thirst, fear, being right, and needing with avoir + bare noun.

use_example.german: Tu as raison, j'ai besoin de manger parce que j'ai faim.
use_example.english: You're right, I need to eat because I'm hungry.

summary.takeaway: In French, you don't 'be' hungry, thirsty, afraid, or right — you 'have' hunger, thirst, fear, and reason.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2901] Have-Hunger & Co): see how The French Mind leads directly into Have-Hunger & Co.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'I am not afraid' (wrap n'...pas around ai before peur):
twist.explanation: Because avoir peur has no article to begin with, the negation is simply Je n'ai pas peur!

faim.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have hunger).
faim.etymology_derivation: French possesses physical states with avoir: avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir froid, avoir chaud, avoir raison.

soif.etymology_derivation: Used with avoir without an article: avoir soif.

peur.context_translation: I am afraid (lit. I have fear).
peur.etymology_derivation: Latin pavor → peur. Feminine abstract noun.

raison.context_translation: You are right (lit. You have reason).
raison.etymology_derivation: To be right in French is to 'have reason'.

besoin.context_translation: I need help (lit. I have need of help).
besoin.etymology_derivation: Triggers dont in relative clauses because of its built-in de.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

jai.etymology_derivation: je + ai with the vowel sacrificed — elision again, the apostrophe marks the cut.

as.etymology_derivation: Pronounced /a/ — the final s stays silent unless followed by a vowel.

très.etymology_derivation: Latin trāns 'across' — très means 'beyond, across the line'. English kept the same root in transmit and transatlantic.

cœur.etymology_derivation: Latin cor/cordis — English kept the root in core, courage ('heart'), accord.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
